INTERPOL Operation Takes Down Sniper Dz Phishing Platform, Arrests Administrator

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 12 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An INTERPOL-led operation last month resulted in the disruption of Sniper Dz, a decade-long phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform, Group-IB said Thursday. The effort, codenamed Operation Ramz, took place between October 2025 and February 2026, and saw authorities from 13 countries in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region making 201 arrests. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Raviral.com Sniper Dz kit endpoints accessed (k_fac.php / track.js) · [LLM] Phishing email click landing on Sniper Dz infrastructure (URL/click correlation) · [LLM] Brand-impersonating phishing pages on abused free-hosting platforms (Sniper Dz pattern) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Sniper Dz seized phishing infrastructure callback (post-takedown beacons) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Sniper Dz seized phishing infrastructure callback (post-takedown beacons) AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts resolving or connecting to Sniper Dz / Joker Dz infrastructure domains seized during INTERPOL Operation Ramz. Any post-takedown beacon to these domains indicates a pre-existing compromise: dormant malware, browser-stored phishing-page bookmarks being clicked, or a victim whose stolen credentials are still being replayed from a host that's reaching the staging infra. Rationale: All 13 domains are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC bundle for Sniper Dz / Joker Dz infrastructure seized by INTERPOL. Any callback to seized infrastructure is high-fidelity because the platform was taken offline in Feb 2026 — legitimate traffic should be zero. Cross-reference with the Group-IB / Unit 42 (Oct 2024) Sniper Dz writeups referenced in the article.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-research sandbox detonation (any.run, Hybrid Analysis worker subnets) resolving seized domains as part of historical sample replay
  • Threat-intel enrichment platforms (Recorded Future, Anomali) doing periodic IOC validation from corporate egress
  • Vulnerability scanners with web-crawl modes hitting the IOC list
  • Researchers / red-teamers replaying old phishing PCAPs in a lab subnet that egresses through corporate proxy
  • Web filters that prefetch / categorize URLs from blocklists they pull themselves
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","smartscreen.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Windows Defender" and DeviceName !startswith "sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "sb-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the initiating process and parent for the connection on the implicated host. Determine whether it's a browser (user clicked an old bookmark / opened an archived email), a sandbox VM, or an unknown process (likely dormant stealer). Check the host's mail history for the URL. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole all 13 domains at the proxy / DNS resolver immediately; this should be a permanent blocklist. Isolate the host if the calling process is non-browser. Force a password reset for the implicated user across SSO and externally-facing brand accounts (PayPal, Facebook, Steam, Netflix) given the credential-theft objective of the platform. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot the host's AAD sign-in history for the past 90 days against impossible-travel / new-MFA-device events. Sweep the org for any other host that resolved any seized domain in the last 180 days using the same IOC list.

Raviral.com Sniper Dz kit endpoints accessed (k_fac.php / track.js) AIDelivery High
Hunts HTTP/S access to two highly-specific Sniper Dz kit URLs documented by Group-IB: `/k_fac.php` (the Facebook-template credential submission endpoint) and `/host_style/style/js-track/track.js` (the per-victim tracking script). Either path appearing on the wire from an internal host is a strong indicator that a user is sitting on a live Sniper Dz phishing page on the seized infrastructure or a mirror. Rationale: `/k_fac.php` and `/host_style/style/js-track/track.js` are kit-specific filenames pulled from the article's IOC bundle (Group-IB analysis of seized raviral.com hosting). These paths have no legitimate use outside the Sniper Dz Facebook phishing template, so a single hit is high-confidence. Combining path-match with host=raviral.com catches mirrored/cloned kits even if the domain changes.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A blue-team detonation lab fetching the IOC URL for signature development
  • Researcher pulling the kit source via curl/wget from a workstation behind the corporate proxy
  • An automated phishing-takedown vendor (PhishLabs, Netcraft) scanning from the corporate IP space
  • Mirror-by-coincidence: an unrelated CMS that happens to expose /k_fac.php — verify the Referer / Host pairing
  • Search-engine crawler image rendering of archived screenshots that embed track.js
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("-IOC","--ioc","threat-intel","sandbox")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For the matching host, pull the full browser session — Referer chain, parent process of the browser tab, and the exact URL preceding the kit-path fetch. If the parent is Outlook/Teams/explorer.exe via a link-click, treat as a confirmed live phishing visit. Step 2 (contain): Block raviral.com plus the two kit paths at the egress proxy. Reset the user's credentials for any brand the kit template impersonated (the article lists PayPal, Facebook, Instagram, Yahoo, Netflix, Steam as primary targets — Facebook is the `_fac` template). Revoke active AAD sessions and require MFA re-enrollment. Step 3 (hunt): Search the prior 48h of EmailEvents for any URL pointing at raviral.com or the other 12 seized domains for this recipient, and pivot across all internal users who received the same NetworkMessageId thread.

Phishing email click landing on Sniper Dz infrastructure (URL/click correlation) AIDelivery High
Correlates Defender for O365 Safe-Links click telemetry against the 13 seized Sniper Dz / Joker Dz domains. A `ClickAllowed` or `ClickedThrough` to any of these URLs proves the user reached a credential-harvesting page — a higher-fidelity signal than passive email delivery alone. Rationale: Joins inbound delivered email containing any of the 13 article-listed Sniper Dz domains to a Safe-Links click event proving the user actually reached the credential-capture page. The IOC list is verbatim from the article's pre-extracted bundle. Falcon LogScale left empty: FDR does not ship M365 Defender email/URL-click telemetry.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security awareness training platforms (KnowBe4, Cofense PhishMe) using these domains as decoys in simulated phishing — filter by known campaign sender
  • Threat-intel analysts forwarding phishing samples to a shared mailbox, then clicking from a triage console
  • User submits a phishing report through the Outlook 'Report Phish' button which clicks the URL in a sandboxed renderer
  • Mail with the URL gets archived to a researcher's quarantine inbox and the link is opened from there
  • Press-release / news article that legitimately links to a sniperdz.com forensic summary
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("phishreport@contoso.com","abuse@contoso.com","soc@contoso.com") and IPAddress !in ("<known SOC sandbox egress IP>","<KnowBe4 simulator egress>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the NetworkMessageId from the click and inspect EmailEvents for sender authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), DeliveryLocation, and whether other recipients in the same thread also clicked. Look up the user's role in IdentityInfo to assess credential-blast-radius. Step 2 (contain): Force a password reset and revoke active sessions for the clicking user via Azure AD. Soft-delete the message from all recipients with Threat Explorer / `Soft-Delete`. Add the matched URL+domain to the tenant block list. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot AADSignInEventsBeta for the clicking user looking for sign-ins within 2-6h of the click from unusual countries / new IPs / non-compliant devices. Sweep EmailEvents for any other inbound mail with URLs to the 12 sibling domains within the last 30d.

Brand-impersonating phishing pages on abused free-hosting platforms (Sniper Dz pattern) AIDelivery Medium
Hunting query for the structural signature of Sniper Dz phishing pages: brand keywords (PayPal, Facebook, Instagram, Netflix, Steam, Yahoo, Free Fire / Garena, PUBG — the named targets in the article) embedded in the subdomain or path of free-hosting platforms (github.io, netlify.app, glitch.me, pantheonsite.io, 000webhostapp.com, epizy.com, blogspot.*). Surfaces unseen Sniper Dz / Joker Dz mirrors that re-spawn after the seizure, plus copycat PhaaS using the same hosting playbook. Rationale: Pattern extracted from the 13 article-listed Sniper Dz IOCs: 8 of them are brand- or lure-keyword subdomains on free hosting (github.io, netlify.app, glitch.me, pantheonsite.io, 000webhostapp.com, epizy.com, blogspot.be). Article says the platform deployed 80 templates across 30 brands in 5 languages and 20,000+ domains have been associated — first-seen hunting against this signature catches mirrors and copycat PhaaS operators using the same playbook.
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate brand-run microsites on Netlify/Vercel (some companies host promo pages this way) — verify by checking SSL cert SAN list
  • Researchers/students publishing fan sites or CTF write-ups containing brand names
  • Open-source projects hosted on GitHub Pages with names that coincidentally include 'login' or 'secure'
  • Legitimate gaming-community sites for Free Fire / PUBG / Garena hosted on free platforms — common in MENA / SEA
  • Brand-protection vendors crawling these patterns from corporate egress
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !startswith "https://docs." and RemoteUrl !startswith "https://help." and RemoteUrl !contains "/issues/" and RemoteUrl !contains "/blob/" and RemoteUrl !contains "/pull/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each first-seen hit, render the URL in a sandbox and verify it's a credential-capture page; check the page source for `track.js`, `k_fac.php`, or form posts to raviral.com / sniperdz.com infrastructure (same template family). Pull WHOIS / GitHub repo owner if applicable. Step 2 (contain): Block the domain at the proxy. If users from your org reached the page, force credential reset for the impersonated brand's corporate SSO (if applicable) and revoke active sessions. Report to the hosting provider's abuse endpoint (GitHub, Netlify, Glitch all have rapid takedown). Step 3 (hunt): Extend the baseline window to 180d to surface long-tail Sniper Dz mirrors. Pivot the malicious URL into EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo to find the delivery vector and the full recipient list.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Europol Disrupts AudiA6 Crypto Laundering Service Used by Ransomware Gangs

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Authorities in Europe have disrupted AudiA6, a cryptocurrency laundering service used by ransomware gangs and cybercriminal networks. Europol, in a statement issued Thursday, said the dismantling of AudiA6 cut off a "key financial pipeline used to wash hundreds of millions in illicit profits." The service is estimated to have been used to launder more than €336 million (~$389 million) since the

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1486 T1528
Domainsdesignli.pictures pheontx.eu smplfy.in sumato-soft.org technobrains.dev lett.email trayo.app deliverly.top inboxly.top postfast.eu

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound or outbound email involving AudiA6 mule-recruitment domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/network contact with AudiA6 money-mule registration domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DNS/network contact with AudiA6 money-mule registration domains AICommand & Control High
Detects endpoints resolving or connecting to the 19 email-infrastructure domains Europol linked to the AudiA6 crypto-laundering service. These domains were used to register fraudulent KYC accounts at cryptocurrency exchanges; a corporate device touching them indicates either an insider acting as a money mule, attacker reuse of corporate infrastructure for laundering, or recruitment communications reaching staff. Rationale: All 19 domains are taken verbatim from the Europol statement in the article body — they are confirmed by a primary law-enforcement source naming them as AudiA6-controlled infrastructure for mule account registration. No second-source web search was performed; the IOC list IS the primary-source bulletin. The domains are unusual second-level / vanity TLDs (.pictures, .top, .click, .agency, .express, .black, .email) so corporate baseline noise is near-zero, justifying alerting tier.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the Europol seizure page or VirusTotal pivot from a security workstation
  • Compliance / fraud team performing mule-account research against the published domain list
  • Researcher visiting the post-takedown Europol seizure banner now hosted on the seized domains
  • Honeypot / sinkhole resolution sweeps from a security tooling host enumerating IOC lists
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountName !has_any ("soc","threatintel","fraud","compliance")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the resolving process and user — if InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser and the user belongs to security / fraud / compliance, check if they were actively reviewing the Europol bulletin (corroborate with browser history or ticket activity). Pull the device's user-context: insider risk score, finance/payments role, prior crypto-exchange traffic. Step 2 (contain): if the user is not a security researcher, isolate the device via Defender / Falcon Network Containment, suspend the AAD account, and block all 19 domains at the proxy/DNS layer pending review. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the device's last 30 days for outbound traffic to crypto-exchange APIs (binance, kraken, coinbase, kucoin), email to/from these same domains, and any KYC document uploads from the device; also sweep the org for any other host that resolved the same domain.
let AudiA6Domains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend HostLower = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where HostLower has_any (AudiA6Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let AudiA6Domains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | extend QueryLower = tolower(DnsQuery) | where QueryLower has_any (AudiA6Domains) | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Query = DnsQuery, ResponseCode = DnsResponseCodeName, Source = "ImDnsActivity"),
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | extend QueryLower = tolower(Name) | where QueryLower has_any (AudiA6Domains) | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname = Computer, SrcIpAddr = ClientIP, Query = Name, ResponseCode = ResultCode, Source = "DnsEvents")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound or outbound email involving AudiA6 mule-recruitment domains AIDelivery High
Detects email events where the sender or recipient domain matches one of the 19 AudiA6-controlled email domains identified by Europol. Article specifies these domains were used to register money-mule cryptocurrency exchange accounts using stolen identities and that Russian-speaking intermediaries were recruited via them — corporate email touching these domains indicates either mule-recruitment outreach or a staff member operating accounts on behalf of the laundering ring. Rationale: Article explicitly states AudiA6 'relied on both commercial email providers and email addresses linked to domains under their control to register money mule accounts' and recruited 'Russian-speaking intermediaries' via these channels — so inbound mail FROM these domains is recruitment outreach and outbound mail TO them is staff operating as mules. Sentinel KQL left empty because the provided Sentinel schema reference does not list a clean mailflow table (OfficeActivity covers admin operations, not full inbound metadata); operators on M365D-connected Sentinel tenants can re-use the Defender query verbatim against the imported EmailEvents table. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as none of those platforms ship M365 mailflow telemetry in the schemas referenced. Sigma skipped because Sigma's email logsource has no portable cross-vendor sender-domain selector matching this shape.
ATT&CKT1585.002 T1566
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Anti-fraud or threat-intel team mailing the AudiA6 domains for IOC validation / takedown coordination
  • A legitimate small SaaS that shared infrastructure on a generic vanity TLD (low risk given Europol seizure but possible for residual MX records on .email/.top domains)
  • Researcher subscribing a personal corporate mailbox to a blog newsletter that happens to send from one of the seized vanity domains pre-takedown
  • Quarantined / blocked spam that EmailEvents still records as a delivery attempt (DeliveryAction == Blocked) — analyst should treat these as a hit but lower severity
Suppression filter
| where not (RecipientEmailAddress has_any ("abuse@","soc@","threatintel@","fraud@") and EmailDirection == "Inbound")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full message body via Threat Explorer / Content Search, check EmailDirection (Inbound = likely recruitment, Outbound = potential mule activity by the user). Examine sender display name, language (article notes Russian-speaking intermediaries), and any crypto-wallet addresses or exchange-platform links in the body. Step 2 (contain): if Outbound from an internal user, suspend the AAD account and seize the mailbox for forensics; if Inbound and delivered, soft-delete from all recipient mailboxes via Threat Explorer and add the sender domain to the tenant block-list. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the recipient/sender user — pull their 90-day SigninLogs for unusual geo, AAD app consents to crypto-wallet/exchange OAuth apps, and any DLP hits on outbound files containing identity documents (passport scans, utility bills) which are the KYC artifacts AudiA6 needed for mule registration.
let AudiA6Domains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| extend SenderDom = tolower(SenderFromDomain), SenderMailDom = tolower(SenderMailFromDomain), RcptDom = tolower(tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress, "@")[1]))

| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, EmailDirection, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes, UrlCount, AttachmentCount
| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

SecurityEvent

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

ShinyHunters Exploits Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day (CVE-2026-35273) to Breach Universities

The Hacker NewsCISA KEV
2026-06-12 17 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion crew exploited an unpatched flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft to break into enterprise systems, steal data, and demand payment to keep it private. The campaign hit universities hardest. Google's Mandiant attributes it to the group it tracks as UNC6240, and dates the activity between May 27 and June 9. Oracle did not publish its advisory until June 10, so the bug was a

Oracle PeopleSoft PSEMHUB / PSIGW exploitation attempt (CVE-2026-35273) AIExploitation High
External HTTP POSTs against the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (/PSEMHUB/hub) or the Integration Gateway HTTP listener (/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector) — the two endpoints UNC6240/ShinyHunters used to weaponise the May–June 2026 PeopleTools 8.61/8.62 zero-day. Hunts the entry point Mandiant told customers to perimeter-block. Rationale: Both URI patterns are the Oracle-mitigation paths in the article — `/PSEMHUB/hub` is the exploited servlet, `/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector` is the secondary endpoint Mandiant told ops to firewall. POST + 2xx/3xx is the success signature.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PeopleSoft Environment Management Agent (PSEMAgent) on internal subnets POSTing to /PSEMHUB/hub
  • SOAP/REST integrations hitting /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector from approved partner IPs
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7) probing the same endpoints
  • Internal monitoring tools (Site24x7, Datadog synthetics) health-checking the gateway
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ((_GetWatchlist('PeopleSoft_Approved_Sources') | project IP)) and csUserAgent !has_any ("PSEMAgent", "Tenable", "Qualysguard", "Nessus")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull `cIP` against approved PSEMAgent / partner / scanner allowlists; map the host to an environment (prod/test). Inspect the POST body and `csUriQuery` for XMLDecoder gadgets or class-loader chains. 2) Contain: at the perimeter, block external access to `/PSEMHUB/*` and `/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector` per Oracle's June-10 advisory; on single-server installs remove PSEMHUB.war. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC `Webshell Drop Under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war` and `XMLDecoder Persistence` on the targeted server for follow-on artifacts, and to UC `UNC6240 C2 Contact` for outbound calls from the same host.
// Targets WebLogic/IIS access logs. Adapt the table to your weblogic syslog/custom collector if PeopleSoft is fronted by Linux Apache/Nginx.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub", "/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector")
| where scStatus in (200, 201, 202, 204, 301, 302)
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Paths = make_set(csUriStem), UAs = make_set(csUserAgent) by Computer, cIP
| order by LastSeen desc

Webshell drop under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war (UNC6240 staging artifacts) AIInstallation High
Detects unexpected .jsp files written under `PSEMHUB.war`, and creation of the article-specific staging folders (`logs`, `persistantstorage` [sic], `scratchpad`) under PSEMHUB paths. These are the direct post-exploitation persistence artifacts Mandiant called out in the CVE-2026-35273 hunt guidance. Rationale: Three article-specific predicates: .jsp under PSEMHUB.war (Oracle ships zero JSPs there by default), and the misspelt `persistantstorage` plus `scratchpad`/`logs` folder names Mandiant fingerprinted from the exposed UNC6240 staging boxes. The typo alone is gold.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Oracle CPU/PSU patch deployment unpacking new JSPs into PSEMHUB.war (rare; gated to maintenance windows)
  • Admin-driven Environment Hub redeployment via psadmin (parent process will be java/psadmin, off-hours unusual)
  • Custom in-house PeopleTools extensions pushed via change-management
  • Backup/AV temporary file extraction into the webapps directory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("psadmin", "psadmin.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-deploy", "-patch"))
| where Timestamp !between (todatetime('2026-06-10T00:00:00Z') .. todatetime('2026-06-10T23:59:59Z'))  // exclude Oracle advisory-day legitimate patching
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the .jsp / folder and pivot on `InitiatingProcessFileName` — patch deploys come from `java`/`psadmin` during change windows; webshells come from `java` reacting to inbound HTTP. Check parent web request in WebLogic access log within ±60s for a matching `/PSEMHUB/*` POST. 2) Contain: take the file offline (copy for forensics), quarantine the host, kill the WebLogic JVM, and block `/PSEMHUB/*` externally. 3) Hunt: query `UNC6240 C2 Contact` for outbound calls from the same `DeviceId`, and `Outbound SMB 445 from PeopleSoft Host` for NetNTLM coercion off the same box.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has "PSEMHUB.war" and FileName endswith ".jsp")
   or (FolderPath has_any ("PSEMHUB/persistantstorage", "PSEMHUB.war/persistantstorage", @"PSEMHUB\persistantstorage",
                            "PSEMHUB/scratchpad",       "PSEMHUB.war/scratchpad",       @"PSEMHUB\scratchpad",
                            "PSEMHUB/logs",             "PSEMHUB.war/logs",             @"PSEMHUB\logs"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has "PSEMHUB.war" and TargetFileExtension =~ "jsp")
   or  TargetFilePath has_any ("PSEMHUB/persistantstorage", "PSEMHUB.war/persistantstorage",
                                "PSEMHUB/scratchpad",       "PSEMHUB.war/scratchpad",
                                "PSEMHUB/logs",             "PSEMHUB.war/logs")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PeopleSoft XMLDecoder persistence via envmetadata XML write AIInstallation High
Hunts modifications to `.xml` files under the PeopleSoft web doc root `envmetadata/data/environment` path — the XMLDecoder gadget persistence the article warns triggers on next WebLogic restart. Distinct from the .jsp webshell pivot, this is the boot-time persistence pivot. Rationale: Article verbatim: "recently changed .xml files under the web doc root's envmetadata/data/environment, which can be abused for XMLDecoder persistence that fires on the next restart." These XMLs are normally read-only after install — any write is suspicious by definition.
ATT&CKT1505 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PeopleTools environment metadata regeneration during a domain reconfigure
  • Backup software touching the file (read-not-write differentiates)
  • Patch deployment (rare; should fall in a change window with psadmin parent)
  • Configuration-management tool (Ansible/Puppet) pushing a custom env definition
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-configure", "reconfigure", "applyEnvironmentSettings") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the touched XML against the last-known-good (Oracle ships pristine envmetadata content per release; any change should match a change ticket). Look for `<java>`, `<object class="java.beans.XMLDecoder">`, or class-instantiation gadgets. 2) Contain: revert the file from backup, restart WebLogic only after the file is clean, and block external `/PSEMHUB/*`. 3) Hunt: same host for `UNC6240 C2 Contact` and `Webshell Drop Under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war`; identify the WebLogic access-log POST that preceded the file write.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("envmetadata/data/environment", @"envmetadata\data\environment")
| where FileName endswith ".xml"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("envmetadata/data/environment", @"envmetadata\data\environment")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "xml"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNC6240 / ShinyHunters C2 contact — azurenetfiles.net or PSEMHUB staging IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound DNS or TCP connections from any host to the UNC6240 C2 domain `azurenetfiles.net` (Azure NetApp Files lookalike), the five sequential staging IPs 142.11.200.186-190 (Python SimpleHTTP on port 8888), and the two other staging IPs Mandiant enumerated. Single high-fidelity IOC list. Rationale: Seven hard IOCs straight from the article: domain `azurenetfiles.net`, IP block 142.11.200.186-190 (sequential, Python SimpleHTTP:8888), plus 108.174.202.99 and 176.120.22.24. These were Mandiant-triaged exposed staging boxes, not WHOIS speculation.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tooling that resolves IOCs from a SIEM host (filter on the TI-collector host)
  • Researcher / IR analyst on a sandbox host actively investigating the campaign
  • Legitimate Azure NetApp Files customer accidentally typo'd in a config (the real domain is azure.netapp.com)
  • Security training labs replaying the IOC for tabletop exercises
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ((_GetWatchlist('TI_Research_Hosts') | project HostName)) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sentinelone-agent", "defender-mp", "threatconnect", "misp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on the source host — is it a PeopleSoft server (high-priority), an analyst sandbox (deprioritise), or a user endpoint (lateral risk)? Pull the initiating process and parent. 2) Contain: sinkhole `azurenetfiles.net` at the resolver; block all seven IPs at the perimeter and egress proxy; isolate any PeopleSoft host that hit them. 3) Hunt: feed the source host through `Webshell Drop Under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war`, `XMLDecoder Persistence`, and `SSH Fanout Script Execution`. Pull DNS history 90 days back for the domain — pre-zero-day reconnaissance pivots.
let UNC6240_IPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
let UNC6240_Domains = dynamic(["azurenetfiles.net"]);
union
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(45d)
   | where RemoteIP in (UNC6240_IPs)
        or RemoteUrl has_any (UNC6240_Domains)
        or (RemotePort == 8888 and RemoteIP startswith "142.11.200.")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
             InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(45d)
   | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
   | where RemoteUrl has_any (UNC6240_Domains)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort = int(null), RemoteUrl,
             InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let UNC6240_IPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
let UNC6240_Domains = dynamic(["azurenetfiles.net"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
   | where DstIpAddr in (UNC6240_IPs)
        or DstHostname has_any (UNC6240_Domains)
        or (DstPortNumber == 8888 and DstIpAddr startswith "142.11.200.")
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (UNC6240_Domains)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr = "", DstPortNumber = 0, DstHostname = DnsQuery, NetworkProtocol = "DNS", NetworkBytes = 0)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound SMB (TCP/445) from PeopleSoft host to public IP — NetNTLM coercion AIExploitation High
Hunts outbound TCP/445 from PeopleSoft application servers to public destinations. Article states the CVE-2026-35273 exploit chain may coerce machine-account NetNTLM authentication to attacker SMB to harvest hashes — a Linux-or-Windows-host SMB egress to internet is the giveaway. Rationale: Article verbatim: "Outbound SMB traffic on port 445 from PeopleSoft hosts to external destinations, which the exploit chain may use to capture machine-account NetNTLM hashes." PeopleSoft servers have zero legitimate need to reach internet SMB.
ATT&CKT1187 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured backup agent (Veeam/Commvault) pointed at a cloud SMB target
  • Legitimate Azure Files / AWS FSx integration where /etc/fstab mounts a cloud SMB share (filter by destination)
  • Penetration test simulating Responder/Impacket coercion
  • Network monitoring scanner doing reachability probes to RFC-1918-leaked public IP
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ((_GetWatchlist('Approved_Cloud_SMB_Endpoints') | project IP)) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeamagent", "commvault-cvd", "netbackup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm host is a PeopleSoft app/web server; capture the initiating process — `java` or unknown is malicious, `mount.cifs`/`smbclient` with a known backup target is likely benign. 2) Contain: drop the 445 session at the egress firewall, force-rotate the host's machine account password (Linux: keytab regeneration; Windows: `klist purge`+`netdom resetpwd`). Block external 445 from the PeopleSoft VLAN. 3) Hunt: rerun `UNC6240 C2 Contact` and check authentication logs (Sentinel SecurityEvent 4624/4625) for the machine account succeeding from unusual sources in the next 7 days.
let PeopleSoftHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSAPPSRV", "PSPRCSRV", "PSEMHUB", "psadmin", "tuxedo", "WebLogic", "PSAESRV")
       or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSAPPSRV", "PSPRCSRV", "PSEMHUB", "psadmin", "tuxedo")
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 445 and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where DeviceId in ((PeopleSoftHosts | project DeviceId))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let PeopleSoftHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSAPPSRV", "PSPRCSRV", "PSEMHUB", "psadmin", "tuxedo", "WebLogic", "PSAESRV")
       or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSAPPSRV", "PSPRCSRV", "PSEMHUB", "psadmin")
    | distinct DvcHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 445
| where DvcHostname in ((PeopleSoftHosts | project DvcHostname))
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| ComputerName=/(psoft|peoplesoft|psapp|psweb)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

ShinyHunters marker file dropped into PeopleSoft directories AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the exact UNC6240 marker file `README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT` anywhere on disk. The `[victim]_fanout.sh` script drops it into PeopleSoft directories as the attacker's calling-card. Filename is unique enough that a single sighting is high-confidence. Rationale: Literal article string. Filename is sufficiently unique that incidental collisions are near-zero — any hit is treated as confirmed UNC6240 compromise unless a researcher/honeypot is in-scope.
ATT&CKT1491.001 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-researcher copying the IOC to a sandbox/test VM
  • Honeypot deployment of the filename for canary purposes
  • Backup restore of a previously-compromised filesystem image (look at file timestamp vs restore window)
  • IR analyst pulling forensic copies onto a triage host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ((_GetWatchlist('IR_Sandbox_Hosts') | project HostName))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm host role and whether the filename is on a known sandbox/canary/IR-triage system; if not, treat as confirmed UNC6240 compromise. Capture full file contents — UNC6240 often embeds victim ID. 2) Contain: isolate the host from network, force-rotate all credentials cached on the box, snapshot for forensics, and disable any service-account creds that touched the box in the last 30 days. 3) Hunt: across all assets, sweep for `UNC6240 C2 Contact`, `Webshell Drop Under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war`, `SSH Fanout Script Execution`, and `Outbound SMB 445 from PeopleSoft Host`. Notify legal/comms — ShinyHunters publishes to a leak site.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(45d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data staging — zstd execution followed by outbound SSH from PeopleSoft host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates `zstd` compression on a PeopleSoft host with outbound SSH (TCP/22) to a public destination within 30 minutes. Article's command-history reveal: UNC6240 compressed loot with zstd and SSH'd it out to the ShinyHunters leak-site mirror server. Rationale: Article verbatim: "the data compressed with zstd and an outbound SSH connection to the server hosting the public mirror of the ShinyHunters leak site." zstd on PeopleSoft app servers is rare; pairing it with public-IP SSH within 30 min isolates the staging→exfil chain.
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1048.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin tarballing logs with zstd for vendor support ticket (followed by SCP/SFTP to vendor)
  • Backup tool using zstd then rsync-over-SSH to off-site DR target
  • Developer SSH to GitHub/GitLab from a build host that happens to be PeopleSoft-adjacent
  • Patch/package management using zstd (some Linux package managers — filter on user==root + apt/dpkg parent)
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ((_GetWatchlist('Approved_Backup_DR_Endpoints') | project IP)) and SshProcess !in~ ("rsync", "scp", "sftp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the `DstIpAddr` against approved off-site backup / vendor support destinations; geolocate; inspect `ZstdCmd` for source paths — anything reading from PS_HOME, PS_APP_HOME, database dump dirs is a strong indicator. 2) Contain: drop the SSH session at the egress firewall, snapshot the host, capture netflow for the last 24h, and notify the data-loss-incident team. 3) Hunt: query the same DeviceId for `UNC6240 C2 Contact`, `Marker File Drop`, and any prior `Webshell Drop Under PeopleSoft PSEMHUB.war`. Sweep for similar zstd+SSH patterns across the PeopleSoft fleet over the last 30 days.
let ZstdExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FileName =~ "zstd" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(^|\s|/)zstd(\s|$)"
    | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
    | project ZstdTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ZstdCmd = ProcessCommandLine, ZstdProcessId = ProcessId;
let SshOut = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemotePort == 22 and RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project SshTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
              RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
ZstdExec
| join kind=inner SshOut on DeviceId
| where SshTime between (ZstdTime .. ZstdTime + 30m)
| project ZstdTime, SshTime,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SshTime, ZstdTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, ZstdCmd, RemoteIP,
          SshProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, SshCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by ZstdTime desc
let ZstdExec = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ActingProcessName endswith "zstd" or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(^|\s|/)zstd(\s|$)"
    | project ZstdTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ZstdCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
let SshOut = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where DstPortNumber == 22
    | where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
    | project SshTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, NetworkBytes;
ZstdExec
| join kind=inner SshOut on DvcHostname
| where SshTime between (ZstdTime .. ZstdTime + 30m)
| project ZstdTime, SshTime,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SshTime, ZstdTime),
          DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ZstdCmd, DstIpAddr, NetworkBytes
| order by ZstdTime desc
source:linux.auditd (@process.command_line:*zstd* OR @process.executable.name:zstd OR @process.executable.path:*/zstd) NOT @process.command_line:*--decompress* NOT @process.command_line:*-d*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\/zstd$/i OR CommandLine=/(^|\s|\/)zstd(\s|$)/i)
| NOT CommandLine=/-d(\s|$)/i
| NOT CommandLine=/--decompress/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, UserName], function=count())
