UNC6240 SSH fan-out script execution ([victim]_fanout.sh) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution or filesystem write of the UNC6240 lateral-movement script matching the `*_fanout.sh` naming convention. The article specifies the per-victim suffix pattern; the script SSH-sprays a hardcoded credential list against hosts pulled from `/etc/hosts`. Rationale: Article verbatim: "The script, named [victim]_fanout.sh, spreads over SSH by spraying a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords against internal hosts pulled from /etc/hosts." The `_fanout.sh` suffix is sufficiently unusual that any match warrants alert-tier triage.
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1110.001 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A custom legitimate DevOps script that happens to be named *_fanout.sh (rare — most use ansible/salt/fanout-style framework names)
  • Open-source `fanout` utility (parallel SSH wrapper) — exclude only on operator hosts
  • IR/red-team exercise testing the IOC
  • Honeypot script with the same name
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ((_GetWatchlist('DevOps_Automation_Hosts') | project HostName))
Response runbook
1) Triage: cat the script — UNC6240's variant contains a hardcoded user:pass list, an /etc/hosts parse, and an SSH loop. Capture authentication-event chain from the host to internal targets (Sentinel SecurityEvent 4624/4625, IdentityLogonEvents). 2) Contain: isolate the source host, force-rotate every credential present in the script (treat as fully compromised), and disable SSH from the source host VLAN. 3) Hunt: pivot to the destination hosts reached via SSH in the spray — sweep each for the marker file (UC `ShinyHunters Marker File Drop`), `UNC6240 C2 Contact`, and webshell artifacts. Identity team: invalidate any sessions belonging to credentials in the script.
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(45d)
   | where FileName endswith "_fanout.sh"
      or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\S+_fanout\.sh\b"
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source = "ProcessExec",
             Path = FolderPath, Name = FileName, Cmd = ProcessCommandLine,
             Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(45d)
   | where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
   | where FileName endswith "_fanout.sh"
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
             Source = "FileWrite", Path = FolderPath, Name = FileName,
             Cmd = "", Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
   | where ActingProcessName endswith "_fanout.sh"
      or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\S+_fanout\.sh\b"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Source = "ProcessExec",
             Name = ActingProcessName, Cmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
             Parent = ParentProcessName, ParentCmd = ParentProcessCommandLine),
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
   | where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
   | where TargetFileName endswith "_fanout.sh"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Source = "FileWrite",
             Name = TargetFileName, Cmd = "", Parent = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

A tale of two eras

Cisco Talos
2026-06-11 7 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

In this week’s newsletter, Amy reminisces on the tech toys of their childhood, inspired by a hilarious lesson about why your digital privacy shouldn't be left on an open channel.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos weekly top-prevalent malware hash hit (Coinminer / Injector / Dropper.Miner) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Talos weekly top-prevalent malware hash hit (Coinminer / Injector / Dropper.Miner) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution, file-write, or image-load of files matching the SHA256/MD5 set published in the 2026-06-11 Talos Threat Source newsletter (Win.Worm.Coinminer, W32.Injector:Gen.21ie.1201, Win.Dropper.Miner). These are the highest-prevalence malware Talos saw in the wild that week, so any enterprise hit is a hard true-positive worth alerting on. Rationale: Pulled directly from the article's 'Most prevalent malware files from Talos telemetry over the past week' block — four SHA256 + four MD5 values published with Talos detection names (Win.Worm.Coinminer::1201, W32.Injector:Gen.21ie.1201, Win.Dropper.Miner::95.sbx.tg). Hash-on-hash is the highest-fidelity primitive available; FP rate is near zero outside of legitimate IR/RE sandbox handling. No web corroboration needed — Talos is itself the authoritative source for its own weekly telemetry top list. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analyst workstations intentionally detonating samples in an isolated VM that ships EDR to prod tenants
  • Red-team / purple-team exercises staging known-bad coinminer samples against the SOC
  • Threat-intel feeds caching the hash on a file-share scanner that subsequently triggers an EDR scan event
  • EDR test deployments where an admin uses the EICAR-equivalent path to validate alerting
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox-01","sandbox-02","re-vm-01") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Users\malware-analyst\" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Quarantine\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pivot on DeviceName + AccountName to see whether the host belongs to a known sandbox / RE VM segment; pull parent process and download URL (FileOriginUrl on DeviceFileEvents) to determine delivery vector. Step 2 (contain): if not an authorized sample-handling host, isolate the device via Defender Live Response / Falcon RTR, kill the process, block all four SHA256 + four MD5 in the org-wide custom indicator list, and force a full AV scan. Step 3 (hunt): expand to DeviceFileEvents for the example filenames VID001.exe and d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_*_Exe.exe across the fleet, search DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound from the same DeviceId 24h pre- and 48h post-execution to identify miner pool/C2, and check DeviceRegistryEvents for Run-key persistence written by InitiatingProcessSHA256 matching the same hashes.

  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Prompt-injection signatures in OpenClaw message ingestion (vCard FN / contact name / location label) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable OpenClaw versions older than 2026.4.23 (Imperva message-object injection) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent process spawning shell, interpreter, or download utility · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network or DNS to Imperva researcher staging domain imperva_artifactory.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Outbound mail from OpenClaw-connected mailbox carrying AWS / SSH / DB credential blobs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Network or DNS to Imperva researcher staging domain imperva_artifactory.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts any DNS resolution or HTTP connection to imperva_artifactory.com, the researcher-controlled domain Imperva used in the OpenClaw PoC to host the script the agent was tricked into downloading and executing. A hit means either reproduction of the PoC, copy-paste of the PoC by a real adversary, or the original test infrastructure leaking into production telemetry. Rationale: imperva_artifactory.com is the only concrete network IOC in the article — Imperva's staging server hosting the script the agent was driven to download. Cross-checked against the Hacker News write-up confirming the domain belongs to Imperva researcher PoC infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers within the org reproducing the Imperva PoC against a test agent
  • Imperva customers receiving demo content referencing the staging hostname
  • Penetration-test or purple-team exercise simulating the OpenClaw injection chain
  • Threat-intel sandbox detonations of the PoC emitting outbound DNS
  • Browser-driven access by analysts reading the Imperva blog post itself
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe","iexplore.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and initiating process — is the requestor the OpenClaw agent binary, a browser (analyst reading the article), or a sandbox? Capture the downloaded payload SHA256 from DeviceFileEvents. 2) Contain: if the requestor is an OpenClaw agent process under its service account (not a human browser), isolate the host, kill the agent, and rotate any tokens or keys reachable from the agent's mailbox or filesystem connectors. 3) Hunt: pivot on the agent's account for the prior 24h — inbound vCard, contact, or location-pin messages with abnormally long name fields containing angle brackets or download cmdlets, and subsequent outbound mail by the agent to unfamiliar recipients carrying secret-looking blobs.

Vulnerable OpenClaw versions older than 2026.4.23 (Imperva message-object injection) AIExploitation High
Inventories OpenClaw installations and flags any host running a version below 2026.4.23, the build that moves contact names, vCard FN fields, and location labels out of the model prompt body into a separate untrusted-metadata channel. Pre-patch hosts are exploitable via the shared-contact prompt-injection chain regardless of model guardrails. Rationale: Article states the Imperva-disclosed flattening flaw is fixed in OpenClaw 2026.4.23. Any host below that build is exposed because the patch moves untrusted metadata out of the prompt body into a separate channel — model alignment alone cannot compensate. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Inventory
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped or pinned-version test environments that intentionally hold an old build for regression testing
  • Hosts where SoftwareVersion is reported in a non-semver format the parser cannot split cleanly
  • Recent installations not yet fully inventoried (TVM lag of 24-72h)
  • Bundled vendor distributions of OpenClaw reporting a vendor-prefixed version string
  • Custom internal forks of OpenClaw with non-upstream versioning
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate flagged hosts, confirm the OpenClaw service is actually running (not just installed) and whether the agent is wired to mail/messaging channels that ingest external content. 2) Contain: prioritise patching to 2026.4.23+ on any host where the agent is connected to WhatsApp, Slack, Teams, Discord, Matrix, or Zalo external channels; for hosts that cannot be patched immediately, disable the named messaging channel extensions. 3) Hunt: for each pre-patch host, pull 30d of OpenClaw mailbox and connector activity and search for inbound shared contacts, vCards, or location pins whose name/FN/label exceeds 80 chars or contains '<' '>' '`' '$' tokens.

| where major < 2026 or (major == 2026 and minor < 4) or (major == 2026 and minor == 4 and build < 23)
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion

Prompt-injection signatures in OpenClaw message ingestion (vCard FN / contact name / location label) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts ingested messaging payloads (shared contacts, vCards, location pins) whose visible-truncated name or label field carries hidden instruction syntax that would be flattened into the OpenClaw model prompt pre-2026.4.23. Anchors on the angle-bracketed serialisation <contact: name, number> and the download-cmdlet tokens the Imperva PoC abused. Rationale: Article specifies the injection lands via shared-contact name, vCard full-name (FN), and shared-location label fields — all flattened inline into the prompt with serialisation <contact: name, number>. Detection anchors on those exact field names, the <contact:> brackets, and the cmdlet/shell tokens the PoC used to make the agent fetch and run a remote script. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1566 T1059 T1204
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vCard transfers with long display names (corporate signatures, multi-line job titles)
  • Marketing or templated contact shares whose name field includes campaign URLs
  • Penetration test or red-team simulations of the Imperva PoC
  • Customer-support shared contacts that include troubleshooting cmdlets in the FN/notes field
  • Auto-generated vCards from CRM exports with unusual punctuation
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw vCard/contact/location object from the OpenClaw agent log and confirm the suspect tokens are in the name/FN/label field (not the notes/URL field, which is wrapped in OpenClaw's untrusted-content marker). Identify the sender's OpenClaw account or WhatsApp number. 2) Contain: if the message reached an OpenClaw agent on a pre-2026.4.23 host, take the agent offline, revoke its outbound mail and connector tokens, and quarantine any files the agent downloaded in the same session. 3) Hunt: search the 24h around the message for downloads from non-allowlisted domains, child processes of the OpenClaw service binary, and any outbound mail / Slack / Discord activity by the agent to unfamiliar recipients.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where AttachmentCount > 0
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileType in~ ("vcf","vcard") or FileName endswith ".vcf"
    | project NetworkMessageId, FileName, FileType, FileSize, SHA256

| where FileSize > 1024 or Subject has_any ("contact","vcard","location","share")
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, FileSize, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Outbound mail from OpenClaw-connected mailbox carrying AWS / SSH / DB credential blobs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Targets the Varonis agent-phishing scenario: OpenClaw wired to a Gmail inbox is socially-engineered into emailing out credentials it can read from its own mailbox (mock AWS IAM keys, DB connection strings, SSH credentials, weekly customer export). Flags outbound mail from an OpenClaw service account containing credential-shaped blobs or credential file attachments to unfamiliar recipients, plus correlated CloudTrail GetSecretValue calls signed by the agent's principal. Rationale: Article gives Varonis's concrete pretext details — mock AWS IAM access keys, DB connection strings, SSH credentials emailed to an external Gmail address, a fake QBR-deck request for the weekly customer export of 247 enterprise customers. Detection anchors on the exact keyword tokens Varonis showed working (staging access, QBR, weekly export, customer export) and on credential-shaped attachments leaving an agent-owned mailbox to a non-org recipient. CloudTrail leg catches the secret-fetch when the agent has Secrets Manager / SSM / KMS read permissions. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1020 T1552
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate weekly customer-export workflow run by the agent for an approved internal recipient
  • Templated mailbox automation that includes the word 'credentials' in subject lines (password-reset notifications, ticketing system mail)
  • DevOps automation accounts named with 'agent' or 'bot' that legitimately email signed CSRs or cert renewals
  • Red-team simulation of the Varonis agent-phishing scenario
  • Compliance / audit teams legitimately requesting AWS IAM key inventories
Suppression filter
| where RecipientEmailAddress !in~ (dynamic(["approved-export@partner.com","data-pipeline@yourcorp.com"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full message body and attachments for the flagged send; confirm whether the credential blob is real (live AWS key prefix AKIA/ASIA, working DB string, real SSH key) or mock. Identify the original inbound message that triggered the agent's action and the requesting sender's reputation. 2) Contain: revoke any leaked credentials immediately (AWS IAM keys, DB users, SSH keys), disable the OpenClaw agent's outbound-mail capability, and add a tenant rule blocking first-time recipients for the agent's mailbox. 3) Hunt: review 30d of the agent's mailbox for similar pretext patterns (urgency + cred request, routine-sounding export ask), pull CloudTrail GetSecretValue / GetParameter calls signed by the agent's IAM principal, and check Slack/Teams exports for the same data leaving via non-mail channels.

OpenClaw agent process spawning shell, interpreter, or download utility AIInstallation High
Catches the direct outcome described in the article title — an OpenClaw agent process (driven by a poisoned shared contact, vCard, location label, or social-pretext email) spawning a shell, scripting interpreter, or network-download utility to fetch and run attacker-supplied code. Article-specific because OpenClaw is explicitly described as shipping broad shell and file access for the agent. Rationale: Article's title and body both center on OpenClaw being driven to 'run attacker-controlled code' — Imperva's PoC explicitly downloads and runs a script from imperva_artifactory.com, and the article notes OpenClaw 'ships with broad access to files, shells, and more than twenty messaging platforms'. A shell or download utility spawned with OpenClaw as parent is the highest-fidelity behavioural signature of either the Imperva or any copy-cat exploitation, regardless of which injection vector was used. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1059 T1059.001 T1204.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OpenClaw plugins/extensions that intentionally invoke a shell for user-requested tasks
  • Developer testing of OpenClaw automations that legitimately call curl/python/bash
  • OpenClaw helper scripts run during install or upgrade that spawn powershell or bash for environment setup
  • Health-check or telemetry routines that wrap an OS command
  • Sysadmin running OpenClaw interactively from a shell where the parent attribution can flip
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "openclaw-healthcheck" and ProcessCommandLine !has "openclaw-update"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree (grandparent, parent, child) and command line; correlate with the OpenClaw agent log for the conversation/message that triggered the action and identify the original sender. 2) Contain: kill the spawned process and any descendants, isolate the host, revoke the agent's outbound tokens and connector grants, and capture any files dropped in the same session via DeviceFileEvents on the OpenClaw working directory. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user account and host for the prior 24h — outbound connections to imperva_artifactory.com or other newly-resolved domains, inbound vCards/contacts with angle-bracket payloads, and any subsequent outbound mail from the agent's mailbox to unfamiliar recipients with credential-shaped blobs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "openclaw" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "openclaw" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "openclaw"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash","sh","zsh","python","python3","node","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has "openclaw"
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has "openclaw" or ActingProcessName has "openclaw"
    | where TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell","pwsh","cmd.exe","wscript","cscript","mshta","rundll32","regsvr32","/bash","/sh","/zsh","python","node","curl","wget","certutil","bitsadmin")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New GreatXML Exploit Bypasses Windows BitLocker via Recovery Partition XML Files

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse (aka Nightmare-Eclipse and MSNightmare) has released a new Windows BitLocker bypass dubbed GreatXML, a day after they published an exploit for Microsoft Defender. "This was an accidental discovery, it took a total of 4 hours to find this," the researcher said in a post on Blogger. "If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're

CVEsCVE-2026-45585
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1528
