Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Nx s1ngularity postinstall payload telemetry.js created in @nx node_modules
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — npm v12 delivers one of the biggest security improvements in years
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Suspicious child process spawned by npm/node during package install lifecycle · [LLM] Bun runtime install/download triggered from npm or node lineage (Shai-Hulud signature) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from Node.js / npm / Bun process · [LLM] Mass developer-credential file access by Node/npm subprocess · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Suspicious child process spawned by npm/node during package install lifecycle AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the core attack vector described in the article: an npm/yarn/pnpm install lifecycle hook (preinstall/install/postinstall) spawning a shell interpreter or download utility. This is the path Shai-Hulud, Mini Shai-Hulud, Nx s1ngularity and the axios hijack all walked. Once npm v12 lands and locks down install scripts, any hit here represents either a missing allowlist entry or a malicious package executing during install. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim lifecycle-hook strings ('preinstall','install','postinstall') and the package-manager binaries it names (npm, yarn, npx). The parent+child pivot turns generic shell execution into an article-specific supply-chain signal.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Native-module build steps (node-gyp invoking cmd.exe to drive MSBuild / make)
  • Legitimate postinstall hooks of packages like 'cypress', 'puppeteer', 'esbuild', 'electron' downloading their platform binaries via curl/PowerShell
  • Developer running 'npm run' scripts that intentionally invoke a shell
  • CI agents (Azure Pipelines, GitHub Actions runners) where shell-spawn from npm is the build's normal shape
  • Yarn 'postinstall' steps in monorepos that pre-warm caches via curl
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","@mapbox/node-pre-gyp") and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe")) | where not (FileName =~ "curl.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("electron","cypress","puppeteer","playwright","esbuild","swc","sharp"))
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full parent command line — confirm it's an install lifecycle ('npm install', 'npm ci', 'yarn install', or a script with 'postinstall'/'preinstall' tag) rather than a developer-run npm script. Identify the offending package by walking InitiatingProcessFolderPath back to its node_modules\<pkg>\ root and pull that package.json's scripts field. Contain: if the package is unfamiliar or recently published, isolate the host via Defender Live Response, kill the spawned shell tree, and remove the package from node_modules + package-lock.json; quarantine any payload the shell downloaded. Hunt: pivot on the package name across the org for blast radius, hunt for child credential-access UCs on the same host (TruffleHog spawn, ~/.ssh / ~/.aws / .npmrc reads), and check whether the developer's npm/GitHub tokens were used in the last 24h from unfamiliar IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm.cmd","node.exe","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","npx.cmd")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," ci "," add "," i ","postinstall","preinstall","prepare")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(ParentProcessName) has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\npm.cmd","\\node.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\yarn.cmd","\\pnpm.exe","\\npx.exe","\\npx.cmd")
| where tolower(NewProcessName) has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend ParentLower = tolower(CommandLine)
| where ParentLower has_any ("install"," ci "," add ","postinstall","preinstall","prepare") or true
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime install/download triggered from npm or node lineage (Shai-Hulud signature) AIInstallation High
The Shai-Hulud (Nov 2025) and Mini Shai-Hulud (May 2026) worms named in the article both installed the Bun runtime as their first stage during package setup, then used Bun to run a credential stealer / TruffleHog. Detects npm/node/yarn lineage either invoking the Bun installer (bun.sh, get.bun.sh, npm i -g bun) or spawning bun.exe itself — outside of repos that legitimately depend on Bun. Rationale: Article names Shai-Hulud and Mini Shai-Hulud explicitly as installing 'the Bun runtime during setup' from compromised npm packages — Bun being pulled in by npm/node lineage with no Bun-using repo on the host is a near-zero-FP signal of this exact campaign family.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adopting Bun via 'npm i -g bun' interactively
  • Bun-based projects (Next.js with Bun runtime, Elysia) whose CI installs Bun via curl in setup
  • Dockerfile RUN steps that bootstrap Bun before npm install
  • Bun upgrade triggered by 'bun upgrade' invoked through npm script wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in (allowlist_bun_dev_hosts)) | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "bun upgrade")
Response runbook
Triage: identify which npm package's lifecycle script issued the Bun install — pull the originating node_modules path from InitiatingProcessFolderPath chain, check the package's recent publish history for an unexpected version bump, and confirm the affected host has no legitimate reason to use Bun (no bun.lockb in repos). Contain: isolate the host, kill the bun process tree, remove the offending npm package + rebuild lockfiles, rotate any tokens that lived on the host (npm, GitHub PAT, SSH keys, cloud CLI creds). Hunt: across the org search for the same package@version installed elsewhere in the last 7 days, hunt for follow-on TruffleHog execution and outbound to public-repo creation on github.com from this host's git client.
let BunInstallParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm.cmd","node.exe","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe"]);
let BunHints = dynamic(["bun.sh/install","get.bun.sh","install bun","install -g bun","global add bun","add -g bun","\\bun\\bin\\bun"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (BunInstallParents)
| where FileName =~ "bun.exe"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (BunHints)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (BunHints)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunHints = dynamic(["bun.sh/install","get.bun.sh"," install bun"," install -g bun"," global add bun"," add -g bun","\\bun\\bin\\bun","\\bun.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(ParentProcessName) has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\npm.cmd","\\node.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\npx.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe","\\curl.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe")
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\bun.exe" or tolower(CommandLine) has_any (BunHints)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from Node.js / npm / Bun process AIActions on Objectives High
Both Shai-Hulud variants used TruffleHog to scrape secrets after the postinstall hook ran. TruffleHog is a legitimate OSS tool but its execution from a Node/npm/yarn/pnpm/Bun parent — particularly without a known git-secrets workflow — is a strong indicator of a postinstall credential stealer. Rationale: Article verbatim: Shai-Hulud 'ran TruffleHog to scrape secrets' and Mini Shai-Hulud 'pulled the Bun runtime and ran a credential stealer'. TruffleHog spawn under a Node/npm/Bun parent is the exact behavioural signature.
ATT&CKT1552 T1552.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running TruffleHog as a pre-commit / pre-push git hook on a developer's machine
  • CI/CD pipeline that invokes TruffleHog via npm script for secret scanning ('npm run secrets-scan')
  • Husky / lint-staged hooks that wrap TruffleHog
  • Security researcher manually triaging a suspicious package locally
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("husky","lint-staged","pre-commit","pre-push")) | where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git","--repo","--path") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("/home/","\\Users\\","/root","--filesystem /"))
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full trufflehog command line — legitimate usage scans a specific repo path; postinstall-stealer usage typically scans the user's home directory, AppData, or filesystem-wide. Walk parent chain back to the npm install that triggered it and identify the package@version. Contain: isolate the host, kill the trufflehog process tree, capture stdout/stderr for IR (the worm uploads results); assume every credential touched in the last hour is burned — rotate npm token, GitHub PAT, SSH keys, AWS/cloud keys, browser-stored OAuth tokens. Hunt: search across the org for the same npm package@version, hunt for outbound to api.github.com from this host's git client in the next hour (Shai-Hulud creates public repos to dump secrets), and search GitHub org-wide for newly-created public repos with the leaked-secret signature.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe")
| where FileName =~ "trufflehog.exe"
   or FileName =~ "trufflehog"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\trufflehog.exe" or tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "/trufflehog" or tolower(CommandLine) has "trufflehog"
| where tolower(ParentProcessName) has_any ("\\node.exe","\\npm.exe","\\npm.cmd","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\bun.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mass developer-credential file access by Node/npm subprocess AIActions on Objectives High
After the postinstall hook fires, the Nx s1ngularity payload 'scraped GitHub tokens, npm credentials, SSH keys, and crypto wallets'; Shai-Hulud did the same. Detects a Node/npm/yarn/pnpm/Bun process reading multiple distinct credential / wallet artifact paths in a short window — the signature of an in-process stealer. Rationale: Article's Nx s1ngularity paragraph: postinstall payload 'scraped GitHub tokens, npm credentials, SSH keys, and crypto wallets'. The path list is the exact target set the article names; the threshold of 3 distinct paths from one Node process catches the scrape pattern without firing on legitimate single-file reads.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1555 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GitHub CLI (gh) auth refresh reading ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml and ~/.gitconfig
  • AWS CDK / amplify CLI reading ~/.aws/credentials + ~/.aws/config in a single npm run
  • Docker login flows touching ~/.docker/config.json and ~/.npmrc together
  • SSH agent tools or vscode-remote-ssh reading ~/.ssh/config and id_ed25519 during workspace setup
  • Crypto-dev tooling (hardhat, foundry) legitimately reading wallet keystores
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentCmd has_any ("@aws-amplify","hardhat","foundry","truffle suite","@github/cli","husky install")) | where not (SamplePaths has_count_distinct(2) and SamplePaths has_any ("\\.npmrc"))
Response runbook
Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — legitimate developer tools name themselves (gh, aws, hardhat) in the parent chain; an opaque 'node <some random path>.js' with no developer context is the malicious shape. Cross-reference the file timestamps to a recent 'npm install' / 'npm ci' in the same shell. Contain: isolate the host immediately, assume every credential touched is burned — rotate GitHub PAT/SSH keys, npm token, AWS access keys, any wallet that was read. Snapshot disk before the worm self-deletes. Hunt: pivot to outbound network from the same Node process to identify exfil channel (the article notes both Nx and Shai-Hulud uploaded to public GitHub repos — check for repo creation API calls in the last hour), then enumerate the org for the same npm package@version installed elsewhere.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified","FileOpenedForRead") or isempty(ActionType)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\credentials", @"\.aws\config", @"\.npmrc", @"\.netrc", @"\.docker\config.json", @"\.gitconfig", @"\.config\gh\", @"\AppData\Roaming\gh\", @"Ethereum\keystore", @"Bitcoin\wallets", @"\.config\solana", "MetaMask", @"\.kube\config")
   or FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa","known_hosts","hosts.json","credentials")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize PathsTouched = dcount(FolderPath),
            SamplePaths = make_set(FolderPath, 20),
            SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 20),
            ParentCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
  by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\npm.exe","\\npm.cmd","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\bun.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.ssh\\","\\.aws\\credentials","\\.aws\\config","\\.npmrc","\\.netrc","\\.docker\\config.json","\\.gitconfig","\\.config\\gh\\","AppData\\Roaming\\gh\\","Ethereum\\keystore","Bitcoin\\wallets","\\.config\\solana","MetaMask","\\.kube\\config")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa","known_hosts","credentials")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize PathsTouched = dcount(TargetFilePath),
            SamplePaths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 20),
            ParentCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
  by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\Bun.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\.ssh\\* OR *\\.aws\\credentials* OR *\\.aws\\config* OR *\\.npmrc* OR *\\.gitconfig* OR *\\id_rsa* OR *\\id_ed25519* OR *Ethereum\\keystore* OR *Bitcoin\\wallets* OR *MetaMask* OR *\\.kube\\config*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|npm|yarn|pnpm|bun)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\(\.ssh\\|\.aws\\credentials|\.aws\\config|\.npmrc|\.netrc|\.docker\\config\.json|\.gitconfig|\.config\\gh\\|Ethereum\\keystore|Bitcoin\\wallets|MetaMask|\.kube\\config|id_rsa|id_ed25519)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=PathsTouched))
| PathsTouched >= 3

Nx s1ngularity postinstall payload telemetry.js created in @nx node_modules AIWeaponization Medium
The August 2025 Nx s1ngularity attack named in the article shipped its postinstall payload as 'telemetry.js' inside the compromised Nx package versions. Detects creation of telemetry.js under a node_modules\\nx\\ or @nx\\ path by an npm/node lineage — a direct IOC for that campaign and re-uses of the same drop pattern. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'A stolen publish token pushed malicious Nx versions whose postinstall script, telemetry.js, ran on install.' Filename + parent-directory IOC is narrow enough for an alerting tier even though the file extension is innocuous.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pre-compromise Nx versions that legitimately shipped a telemetry.js (verify against known-good Nx package version + SHA256 list)
  • Internal forks of Nx that retain a benign telemetry.js
  • Developer accidentally restoring an old node_modules from a backup that pre-dates the compromise
  • Test fixtures that mirror node_modules structure for unit tests
Response runbook
Triage: pull the SHA256 of the dropped telemetry.js and compare against the known Nx s1ngularity payload hashes (CrowdStrike, GitHub Advisory GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c, Aikido write-up). Identify the Nx package version installed and the package-lock.json that pinned it. Contain: isolate the host, kill node processes, remove the package + lockfile pin, and rotate every credential the host had access to (GitHub PAT, npm token, SSH, cloud CLIs, crypto wallets). Hunt: search across the org for the same Nx version range in package-lock.json files (and CI runners), check GitHub for any public repos created by users on affected hosts in the past 24h (Shai-Hulud / Nx exfil pattern), and audit the GitHub org's audit log for unusual PAT-driven activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "telemetry.js"
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\nx\", @"\node_modules\@nx\", @"\node_modules\nx-cli\", "/node_modules/nx/", "/node_modules/@nx/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "telemetry.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "\\node_modules\\" or TargetFilePath has "/node_modules/"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\node_modules\\nx\\","\\node_modules\\@nx\\","\\node_modules\\nx-cli\\","/node_modules/nx/","/node_modules/@nx/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\npm.exe","\\npm.cmd","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:

tags:

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Unauthenticated POST to meta-ads-mcp /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to the meta-ads-mcp /mcp JSON-RPC endpoint on port 8080 that lack any Authorization header but receive a 2xx response. Directly operationalises CVE-2026-48039: AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() forwards unauthenticated callers to tool handlers instead of returning 401, so successful 2xx + missing auth = exploitation attempt. Rationale: Article body specifies POST /mcp on default port 8080 with no auth headers returns HTTP 200 instead of 401 (http_auth_integration.py:272). Detection looks for exactly that shape: POST + /mcp + 8080 + 2xx + missing Authorization header. Cross-checked GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48039
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal health-check probes from monitoring (Datadog synthetics, Pingdom) hitting /mcp without auth
  • Developer curl tests during local validation on dev workstations
  • Load-balancer L7 health checks (AWS ALB, Azure App Gateway) probing the path
  • Legacy MCP clients pre-configured for trusted-network use without bearer tokens
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Tenable.io) probing exposed services
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.5","10.0.0.6") // exclude approved monitoring probes
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog-Synthetic","kube-probe","Pingdom","GoogleHC")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the destination host is running pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp (check process / container image tag) and version ≤ 1.0.108. Pull the corresponding /mcp response payload from the proxy/WAF and search for `access_token=` string — if present, the operator token is leaked. 2. Contain: block inbound TCP/8080 to the affected host at the perimeter and rotate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN in the operator's Meta Developer console immediately; revoke all sessions and review Meta Ads account audit log for ad-account changes since the first observed unauth POST. 3. Hunt: pivot on the source IP to surface other recon (scan of nearby ports, repeated `tools/call` JSON-RPC payloads, unique MCP tool names invoked); query Meta Graph API access logs for activity from non-corporate IPs using the leaked token.
// Pivots on outbound connections from internal hosts to a meta-ads-mcp server on 8080.
// Defender does not parse HTTP headers — pair this with a proxy/WAF rule for auth-header absence.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 8080
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","HttpConnectionInspected")
| where RemoteUrl has "/mcp" or AdditionalFields has "/mcp"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 8080
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/mcp"
| where HttpResponseCode between (200 .. 299) or HttpStatusCode startswith "2"
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpResponseCode, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Meta access token pattern leaked in /mcp response body AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Meta Graph API access tokens appearing in HTTP response bodies returned by the meta-ads-mcp server. CVE-2026-48039: when downstream Graph API call errors, api.py:263–269 serialises the raw httpx request_url — including `access_token=` query parameter — back into the JSON-RPC 200 OK response, handing the operator credential to the unauthenticated caller. Rationale: Article body shows the exact leak shape in the PoC: 200 OK JSON-RPC response containing `"request_url": "https://graph.facebook.com/v24.0/me/adaccounts?...&access_token=FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789"`. We hunt the literal `access_token=` substring in /mcp response bodies — that is the realised CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authenticated tool callers receiving the same error shape with their OWN token in the request_url (still a fix-worthy bug, just not external attacker)
  • Internal QA running PoC reproductions against staging
  • DevSecOps tooling deliberately probing for the vulnerability
  • Log-capture systems echoing prior-captured PoC payloads back through the proxy
  • WAF false-flagging legitimate Meta SDK response bodies that contain `access_token` parameter names in non-credential contexts
Response runbook
1. Triage: extract the leaked token value from the response body capture, then call `GET https://graph.facebook.com/debug_token?input_token={token}&access_token={app_token}` to identify the owning app + user + scopes. Confirm whether the source IP is internal/external. 2. Contain: invalidate the leaked token immediately via Meta Developer console (Apps > YourApp > Access Tokens > Revoke) and rotate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var on every meta-ads-mcp instance. Block /mcp at the perimeter until patched (>1.0.108). 3. Hunt: review Meta Ads account audit log for ANY API activity using the leaked token after the leak timestamp (campaign edits, ad-account access grants, billing changes); pivot on source IP to find other targeted MCP servers in the org.
// Defender doesn't capture HTTP response bodies; this surfaces the precursor — a Graph API error-path call from a process that also serves /mcp on 8080.
let McpServers = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where LocalPort == 8080 and ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
    | distinct DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "graph.facebook.com"
| join kind=inner McpServers on DeviceId
| where InitiatingProcessFileName1 == InitiatingProcessFileName
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 8080
| where Url has "/mcp"
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where HttpResponseBodyBytes > 200
| extend ResponseBody = tostring(parse_json(tostring(parse_json(strcat('{"r":', AdditionalFields, '}')).r)).response_body)
| where ResponseBody matches regex @"access_token=[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{40,}"
   or ResponseBody has "request_url" and ResponseBody has "access_token="
| extend LeakedToken = extract(@"access_token=([A-Za-z0-9_\-]{40,})", 1, ResponseBody)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpResponseCode, LeakedToken
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

Outbound graph.facebook.com from non-browser process indicates MCP server token use AICommand & Control Medium
Surfaces outbound HTTPS to graph.facebook.com from non-browser, non-SDK processes — the meta-ads-mcp Python server calls Graph API directly using the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN. Spike or new-process appearance on this path can indicate either the vulnerable server in production or a downstream attacker using the leaked token from another vantage point. Rationale: Article confirms make_api_request() in api.py calls Graph API directly via httpx; the calling process is the Python meta-ads-mcp server (Docker example in PoC). Filtering Python/Node/Docker → graph.facebook.com isolates server-side use (legitimate or attacker-via-leaked-token) from human ad-managers using browsers. Sentinel switched to CommonSecurityLog because ImWebSession has no process-attribution columns. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://developers.facebook.com/docs/graph-api
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Other internal services legitimately integrating with Meta Marketing API via Python SDK
  • Data pipelines pulling Meta Ads metrics nightly (Airbnb, Airflow, dbt jobs)
  • Containerised SDKs in CI/CD running ad-account smoke tests
  • Postman/Insomnia desktop apps invoking Graph API from analyst workstations
  • Custom internal dashboards built on facebook-business Python SDK
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("meta_business_sdk","facebook_business","airflow","dbt-run","approved-marketing-job")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the source host is the meta-ads-mcp server (process tree → uvicorn/python serving the FastAPI app). Inventory whether this host should be talking to Graph API at all and on which schedule. 2. Contain: if the host is the vulnerable meta-ads-mcp, isolate from network and rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN. If the connection is from an unexpected host, treat as token-misuse — invalidate the token via Meta Developer console. 3. Hunt: pivot on the AccountUpn / InitiatingProcessAccountName to find the operator whose token was used; correlate with Meta Ads audit log entries from the same period to spot unauthorised ad-account modifications, campaign edits, or new admin grants.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "graph.facebook.com" or RemoteIP in ("31.13.64.0/19")  // Facebook AS32934 ranges
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe","safari.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","node.exe","docker.exe","dockerd.exe","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn.exe") 
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp","http_auth_integration")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has "graph.facebook.com" or RequestURL has "graph.facebook.com"
| where isnotempty(SourceProcessName)
| where SourceProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe","safari.exe")
| where SourceProcessName has_any ("python","node","docker","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, SourceProcessName, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious MCP tool invocation via JSON-RPC tools/call to /mcp endpoint AIExploitation High
Parses POST bodies to /mcp endpoints for JSON-RPC `tools/call` payloads invoking sensitive Meta Ads MCP tools (get_ad_accounts, create_ad, update_campaign, etc.) without authentication context. Article PoC shows the exact request: `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"tools/call",...,"params":{"name":"get_ad_accounts"}}` — same shape as legitimate calls but with no auth headers. Rationale: PoC in article quotes the exact body: `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"tools/call","id":2,"params":{"name":"get_ad_accounts","arguments":{"limit":1}}}`. We detect the JSON-RPC method `tools/call` + sensitive tool name + missing auth header — the literal exploit signature. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/server/tools/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MCP clients running on trusted network that pre-date Authorization header enforcement
  • Internal smoke-tests against /mcp during deployment validation
  • Penetration testers running approved vulnerability scans
  • Claude Desktop / IDE integrations invoking MCP tools from localhost without bearer auth
  • MCP client SDKs that put auth in a custom header (X-API-Key) rather than Authorization
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1") // localhost MCP clients are expected unauthenticated
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full POST body and the response — if the response contains `access_token=` (per UC 2), this confirms successful exploitation and token leak. Identify which tool was invoked (get_ad_accounts is most common probe). 2. Contain: rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN immediately and upgrade meta-ads-mcp to a patched version (>1.0.108 with confirmed fix); block /mcp at perimeter in the interim. 3. Hunt: enumerate every unique tool_name invoked from the suspicious source IP and check Meta Ads audit log for actions matching those tools (e.g. create_ad → look for new ad creations from API in same time window); review whether any state-changing tools (update_*, create_*, delete_*) were called.
// Defender cannot inspect HTTP bodies. Approximate with byte-size + repeat-rate heuristics on /mcp connections from external sources.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalPort == 8080
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize ConnCount = count(), Hosts = dcount(DeviceId), Sources = dcount(RemoteIP)
    by DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where ConnCount >= 3
| order by ConnCount desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 8080
| where Url has "/mcp"
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| extend Body = tostring(AdditionalFields)
| where Body has "jsonrpc" and Body has "tools/call"
| extend ToolName = extract(@"\"name\"\s*:\s*\"([a-z_]+)\"", 1, Body)
| where ToolName in~ ("get_ad_accounts","get_campaigns","get_ads","create_ad","update_campaign","delete_campaign","get_insights","get_audiences","get_business_users")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, ToolName, HttpResponseCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Meta Ads account manipulation following meta-ads-mcp token leak AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a /mcp unauthenticated POST (UC 1) on a host with subsequent Meta Graph API admin-grant / role-modification calls originating from external IPs — the realised lateral-movement path after CVE-2026-48039 token theft. Detects T1098.001 (Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials) using the stolen long-lived META_ACCESS_TOKEN. Rationale: Article impact section explicitly calls out the chain: 'access the Meta Graph API directly outside the MCP interface' after stealing the long-lived credential. This UC correlates the /mcp probe IP with subsequent admin/role changes on graph.facebook.com — the natural T1098.001 follow-on per the GHSA writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://developers.facebook.com/docs/marketing-api/business-asset-management • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/001/
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Change.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ad-ops admin granting access to a new agency staff member from a coffee-shop IP
  • Automated provisioning workflow assigning roles via API on schedule
  • SaaS partner tools (HubSpot, Marin, Skai) modifying ad-account permissions via OAuth
  • Outsourced marketing agency operating from non-corporate IP space
  • Meta SSO migration / bulk-role-update windows
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in ("<approved-agency-cidr>","<saas-partner-egress>")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the Meta Ads Business Manager audit log for the affected account and confirm the timestamp + source IP of the admin/role change. Compare against the source IP recorded in the UC 1 /mcp probe — exact match is strong evidence. 2. Contain: revoke the newly-added admin / user grant in Meta Business Manager, invalidate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN, and require step-up MFA reauthentication for all Meta workspace admins. Block /mcp at the perimeter until patched. 3. Hunt: enumerate every Meta Ads account managed by the same operator token, audit recent campaign changes (especially budget increases, payment-method changes, conversion-pixel modifications) and treat all changes since the first observed /mcp probe as untrusted until verified by the legitimate admin.

Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the three hard-coded GitHub commit-search query strings the Miasma supply-chain worm uses as its three independent C2 channels (PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, Python payload delivery). These strings have zero legitimate business presence and are the highest-fidelity Miasma indicator available. Rationale: The three strings 'DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom', 'TheBeautifulSandsOfTime' and 'firedalazer' are the hard-coded GitHub commit-search queries each Miasma C2 channel uses (PAT discovery, JS payload, Python payload). They are confirmed by SafeDep's analysis, BleepingComputer's report, and a parallel TheHackerNews write-up. Zero legitimate business processes contain these tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst running these strings through their own grep/search tooling for hunting
  • SOC engineer pasting the IOCs into a script or note file
  • Security researcher cloning or reading SafeDep / Cloudsmith write-ups in a developer IDE that logs URL paths
  • Sandbox / detonation environment intentionally executing a Miasma sample for analysis
  • Automation that ingests OSS-supply-chain advisories and writes IOCs to a database column
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe") and not (FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\detonation\\","\\analyst-tools\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process that emitted the string is not an analyst hunting tool, a CTI ingestion script, or a known sandbox. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain; if the string was in a network URL, identify what process issued the GET against api.github.com/search/commits. 2) Contain: if the originating process is a node/python/git/curl invocation on a developer machine or CI runner, isolate the host from network, revoke any GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems publish tokens and JFrog Artifactory credentials owned by that user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same three strings org-wide; pivot on the parent process and SHA256 to find sibling executions; review the developer's git push history for npm/PyPI/RubyGems package versions published in the last 7d for unexpected new releases or postinstall scripts.
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, Source = strcat("Net:", RemoteUrl);
union ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
union From4688, FromAsim
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts for git clone / npm install / pip install / curl / wget operations that reference the briefly-public 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' GitHub repositories which leaked the worm's source on 2026-06-08. A match means the host has either ingested the leaked toolkit or is being staged with it. Rationale: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' is the exact repository slug SafeDep and BleepingComputer report appeared on GitHub from 2026-06-08 hosting the leaked toolkit. The string is uniquely tied to Miasma and would only surface in dev-tool command lines or proxy URLs when a host is cloning, installing or downloading the leaked source. Cross-checked via SafeDep, BleepingComputer and TheRegister. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel team intentionally cloning the leaked repo into a sandbox for analysis
  • Security researcher fetching the source on a developer workstation for write-up
  • SOAR / TIP ingesting OSS advisory feeds and storing the repo URL as an IOC string
  • Vulnerability scanner or SCA tool fingerprinting against known-malicious repo names
  • Blue-team CTF or training environment seeding the toolkit deliberately
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\") and FolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process that issued the clone/install/fetch — confirm it is not a sanctioned analyst sandbox or CTI ingestion job. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and any subsequent npm/pip postinstall script execution from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node/python child processes spawned within 1 hour of the clone, revoke GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Artifactory publish tokens belonging to the user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the three Miasma C2 commit-search strings (see related UC) on the same host and across the org; review the user's recent package publishes for unexpected versions; check GitHub Actions workflows in any repo they touched for newly-added steps referencing untrusted secrets or external scripts.
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let DevTools = dynamic(["git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (DevTools) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
    | where ProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Network";
union isfuzzy=true ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or TargetProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains MiasmaRepo or DestinationHostName contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, Account = SourceUserName, NewProcessName = "", CommandLine = RequestURL, ParentProcessName = "", Source = "Proxy";
union From4688, FromAsim, FromProxy
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.

Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity

| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| sort - files

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Cybersecurity Stars Awards 2026: Winners Announced Across 95 Categories
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("kernel32.dll", "charmap.exe", "router.elf", "version.dll", "inspect.sys"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("kernel32.dll", "charmap.exe", "router.elf", "version.dll", "inspect.sys"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit supply-chain: update binary spawning unusual child
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER known-sample SHA1 execution or filesystem write · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 connection to ESET-disclosed IPs/domains · [LLM] First-seen connection to recently-registered SPECTRALVIPER-shape C2 domain · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 connection to ESET-disclosed IPs/domains AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound network connection to the eight SPECTRALVIPER C2 IPs and six C&C domains ESET published for OceanLotus's 2024-2026 FireAnt Metakit supply-chain and Vietnamese construction-corp campaigns. High-fidelity because every IOC is a known-bad C2 endpoint with no documented benign use. Rationale: Every IP and domain in this query is a SPECTRALVIPER C&C endpoint published in ESET's Table 2 and IOC bundle for the 2024-2026 OceanLotus campaigns; financemachinelearning.com is explicitly named as the C&C domain for the stable SPECTRALVIPER variant. Match by IP catches direct fallback; match by URL catches HTTPS proxied through hostname.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox / malware-analysis VM intentionally detonating SPECTRALVIPER samples
  • Threat-intel scrapers / Shodan-style researchers actively probing the IOC set
  • Security-tool URL-categorization scans of the malicious domains (e.g. Zscaler, Netskope)
  • Legitimate hosts that happen to be on a shared-IP CDN that now resolves to one of these IPs (rare — most IOCs are bare hosting)
  • DNS sinkhole responses if these domains have been sinkholed by a TI provider
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full process tree from DeviceProcessEvents for InitiatingProcessFileName at the time of the connection — confirm whether the originator is a known good binary (security tooling, sandbox) or an unsigned binary in a temp/AppData path matching SPECTRALVIPER drop patterns. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the device via Defender Live Response or EDR network-isolation, block the matched IP/domain at firewall and EDR network indicator policy, force credential reset for the InitiatingProcessAccountName. 3) HUNT: pivot on DeviceFileEvents for SHA1 against the 20-hash IOC set; query DnsEvents for the other five C&C domains across all hosts in the last 90 days; search for any FireAnt Metakit installs (file path or process name) on neighboring hosts and check their update history for a malicious payload window of Oct-2025 to Mar-2026.

let ioc_domains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (ioc_ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (ioc_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let ioc_ips = dynamic(["139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);
let ioc_domains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
  | where DstIpAddr in (ioc_ips) or DstHostname in~ (ioc_domains) or Url has_any (ioc_domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, EventProduct),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
  | where DestinationIP in (ioc_ips) or DestinationHostName in~ (ioc_domains) or RequestURL has_any (ioc_domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceVendor)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
